young.html: Virginia Woolf was an English writer who spent childhood summers at the seaside, in a house that looked out at a lighthouse. Years later she turned those memories into a novel.

In To the Lighthouse, six-year-old James Ramsay wants more than anything to sail out to the lighthouse tomorrow. His mother says yes, if the weather is fine. His father says the weather won't be fine. James is crushed. The trip doesn't happen. Ten years go by, the family changes, and at last James, now a teenager, sails to the lighthouse with his father. Meanwhile a painter friend, Lily, finally finishes the picture she began long before.

young.cap: The book has three parts. Compare how many pages each takes with how much time it covers.

young.html: Inside a minute. Woolf spent pages on a single moment, telling what each person was thinking. Sit with your family for one minute in silence. Afterward, each person writes or says everything they noticed and thought during that minute. How different were your minutes?

full.html: Virginia Woolf (1882–1941) was the daughter of the writer Leslie Stephen. With her sister and friends she was at the center of London's "Bloomsbury group," and with her husband Leonard she ran the Hogarth Press. Her childhood summers were spent at St Ives in Cornwall, where the house looked out on a lighthouse. Her mother died when Virginia was thirteen. To the Lighthouse (1927) moves those memories to the Isle of Skye in Scotland, and the Ramsays are partly portraits of her parents.
It begins in the middle of a conversation:

full.text: “Yes, of course, if it's fine tomorrow,” said Mrs. Ramsay. “But you'll have to be up with the lark,” she added.

full.html: A few pages later her husband stops at the window:

full.text: “But,” said his father, stopping in front of the drawing-room window, “it won't be fine.”

full.html: The Window covers one afternoon and evening. We move from mind to mind: Mrs. Ramsay knitting and worrying over everyone; Mr. Ramsay, a philosopher, anxious about whether his work will last; the painter Lily Briscoe, unsure she can paint at all; the guests at a dinner party that Mrs. Ramsay, for one evening, makes into a perfect whole. Even the view is seen through a mind:

full.text: For the great plateful of blue water was before her; the hoary Lighthouse, distant, austere, in the midst; and on the right, as far as the eye could see, fading and falling, in soft low pleats, the green sand dunes with the wild flowing grasses on them, which always seemed to be running away into some moon country, uninhabited of men.

full.html: Time Passes is short. The house stands empty for ten years while wind and damp creep in. In a few brief sentences set in square brackets, we learn that Mrs. Ramsay has died suddenly, that a daughter has died young, and that a son has been killed in the Great War. An old cleaning woman, Mrs. McNab, struggles to save the house.

The Lighthouse covers one morning ten years later. Mr. Ramsay at last sails to the lighthouse with James and his sister Cam, now teenagers who resent him; on the way, James finally earns his father's praise. On the lawn, Lily Briscoe returns to her old painting, thinks of Mrs. Ramsay, and with one final line at its center, finishes it.

full.html: Woolf turns the usual novel inside out. A dinner takes many pages; ten years, with three deaths, take a few. What matters is not the clock but how moments live in the mind, and what can be made to last: a dinner, a painting, a memory.

The method is often called "stream of consciousness," a phrase first used by William James. Woolf's version glides from one person's thoughts to another's within a paragraph, so the reader feels a whole household thinking at once.
Waiting for a plot. Very little "happens" on the surface. The events are inner ones: a child's anger, a father's need for praise, a painter's moment of vision.

items: William James, earlier on this ladder, named the "stream of consciousness" in psychology.
Bergson, in this era's philosophy, contrasted clock time with lived time, as Woolf's three parts do.
Proust, whom Woolf read with wonder, also made memory and time his subject.
Joyce's novels, which Woolf read with mixed feelings, also follow minds from within.
Woolf's essay A Room of One's Own (1929) asked why so few women had been able to write; Lily Briscoe, told that women can't paint, is a character of that question.
Why can one evening matter more than ten years?
Was Mr. Ramsay wrong to tell James the truth about the weather?
What can last when people die? A painting? A memory? A family?
How well can we ever know what someone else is thinking?

questions: Mr. Ramsay told James the truth: the weather would be bad. Mrs. Ramsay gave him hope. Who was kinder?
Which moments from your family's summers do you think you'll remember in ten years?
Why do you think Woolf told three deaths in just a few lines?
Lily kept working on her painting for ten years. What have you kept working on?
Is it possible to know what someone else is really thinking?
care: The middle section reports three deaths in a few brief sentences, without detail.
